o1.biggest_strength: It gives honest low-to-high ranges for each fix, all checking out (2,430 to 3,646 tickets, 540 to 1,080 bra returns, £11,830 to £19,770 saved), and adds a real bra fit-check in the delivered email that could stop a return before it starts.
o1.biggest_mistake: Measurement is thin: there is a 10% hold-out but no A/B test of the portal, no guardrail such as time to refund, and no note that returns lag orders, so a day-60 read will be misleading.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Add a 50/50 portal test with a time-to-refund guardrail and a note on return lag, and rank the three fixes in one money table that includes the cost of shipping swaps.

o2.biggest_strength: Strong measurement design: the portal runs 50/50, there is a hold-out, a time-to-refund guardrail and a return-lag caveat, and every working is shown and correct, including the self-selection haircut on the fit finder (684 fewer returns).
o2.biggest_mistake: It gives single-point targets, not the range I asked for, and the £209,600 'sales kept' headline mixes fit-finder returns into refunds avoided. The post-delivery message is a generic swap prompt with no bra fit guidance.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Turn the targets into low/high ranges and give first-time bra buyers a short how-to-check-the-fit message after delivery, before they reach for a return.

reason: Both get the numbers right and fix the three real problems. Output 1 gives me honest ranges and a delivered-email fit check that actually saves bra returns. Output 2 measures more carefully, but it hands me single numbers and a generic swap nudge.
